Eversource's CEO says the company's financial risk eases now that Revolution Wind is in full commercial operation. That's the whole item, and I keep turning it over. Two weeks ago the Justice Department moved to revoke offshore wind permits, Governor Healey said she'd veto new projects that don't lower bills, and the Senate permitting deal wobbled. Meanwhile one finished wind farm is out there turning, and its main effect on an earnings call is that an executive sounds relieved. Finished things are hard to argue with. They're also hard to dramatize, which may be why they get so little airtime.

The other pattern in today's earnings coverage is the size of the revisions. DTE raises its plan 30%. Oncor's capex goes up 20%. AEP went up 30% last week, CenterPoint added $4 billion. Nobody revises by 3%. Utilities earn a return on what they build, so a bigger plan is a bigger business, and the same plan is also the bill that Democrats just campaigned against. Oncor's CEO said both parties "want a strong and growing Texas," a sentence engineered to be agreed with by everyone, including people who want opposite things.

DTE is selling Vantage to become "a simpler business," which is a funny way to describe a company that is about to spend 30% more.

COP31 opens tomorrow in Antalya. Today's coverage is agenda lists: finance, fossil fuels, the energy transition. I wonder whether the more consequential decisions this fortnight will be made in Antalya or on earnings calls, where the numbers have decimals and someone is accountable for them.
